### System:
You are a careful analyst scoring business opportunities. Follow the output format exactly.

### User:
Nodewise is a small startup with a toolkit for exploring large graphs in the browser: fast layouts of millions of nodes, clustering, filtering, and timelines of how a network changes.

Candidate use cases:
E. Compliance graphs for pharma supply chains: Pharma compliance teams describe tracing suppliers as a recurring headache, though they cope with spreadsheets. The job is mostly document extraction and regulatory reasoning, with graph views as a small part; Nodewise lacks most of it. Some of the supplier-mapping work could be reused, but much is specific to pharmaceutical regulation. Exclusive data-sharing agreements with two industry consortia would give Nodewise data no competitor could get. One consortium agreed to a six-week trial with three member companies starting soon.
B. Dependency maps for software teams: Engineering teams find tangled code dependencies painful and often slow, and many have asked for better maps. Turning a codebase into a graph needs parsers for many languages that Nodewise has not built, and its layouts suit only part of the problem. Almost everything built here (importers, layouts for directed graphs, change timelines) would serve nearly every other use case. Free open-source tools already draw dependency graphs and are easy to replicate. A plugin could be in front of a few hundred developers within two months.
H. Influence maps for a political-risk consultancy: The consultancy says mapping influence networks takes its analysts days per report, a real but manageable cost. The toolkit handles the network views, though the consultancy's text sources would need moderate new work. The work is tailored to the consultancy's proprietary report formats and would barely carry over. The consultancy's methods are known in the industry, and its competitors use similar off-the-shelf tools. The consultancy can trial a prototype on its next quarterly report, about a month away.
C. Citation networks for academic librarians: Librarians find citation maps interesting, but most say their current search tools are good enough. Citation networks are exactly the large, clustered graphs the toolkit was built for, with no new capability needed. About half of the work (bibliographic importers, a timeline of growth) would be reusable elsewhere. A curated citation dataset assembled with partner libraries would be hard for others to reproduce. University purchasing runs on yearly budget cycles, so the first real answer would come after more than a year.
D. Live map of a partner marketplace: Sellers on a mid-size online marketplace mention the problem only occasionally and have not asked for a solution. The toolkit covers the visual side, but the analytics the marketplace wants would need some new work. Most of the pipeline (streaming ingestion, live layouts) would be reused by later projects. Every seller who joins adds data that makes the map more useful to the others, a network effect a competitor could not copy. The marketplace offered to put a prototype in front of its sellers next month and share usage numbers weekly.
A. Fraud rings for regional banks: Regional banks lose millions a year to organised fraud rings and their fraud teams say finding them is their top priority. Spotting rings means laying out transaction networks and clustering them, which the toolkit does well, though it would need a connector to banking data. The work is tied to each bank's core-banking formats, so little of it carries over to other projects. Several fraud-analytics vendors exist, but Nodewise's speed on very large networks is a modest advantage. Banks run procurement and security reviews that typically take six to nine months before a pilot.
F. Threat-intel graphs for a large telecom: A large telecom's security team loses significant money weekly to network intrusions and wants a solution urgently. Exploring attack graphs over billions of events is precisely what the toolkit does best. The connectors and investigation views would serve almost every other security or network use case. Large security vendors already sell similar graph views and could match the features quickly. The telecom requires a year-long certification process before any production data can be used.
G. Family-tree visualiser for hobbyists: Genealogy hobbyists enjoy the idea, but none has said they need it and existing apps satisfy most of them. Family trees need specialised layouts and record-matching that the toolkit does not have. Around half of the work (importers, layout options) would be usable elsewhere. Hobbyist apps are common and new entrants appear often, though a large shared tree could become somewhat sticky. A free web version could be posted to hobbyist forums this week and draw feedback within days.

Criteria, each scored 1 to 5:
- speed: Time to signal: how soon Nodewise would learn whether it works (5 = a clear signal within weeks; 1 = a year or more before any signal).
- reuse: Reusability: how much of what is built here serves other use cases (5 = almost all of it is reusable; 1 = a bespoke one-off).
- pain: Market pain: how acute and costly the customer's problem is today (5 = losing serious money or time every week and actively looking for a fix; 1 = a nice-to-have nobody asked for).
- moat: Defensibility: how hard it would be for a competitor to copy the offer (5 = proprietary data or network effects; 1 = trivially copied, free alternatives exist).
- fit: Technical fit: how directly Nodewise's existing toolkit solves it (5 = exactly what the toolkit already does; 1 = needs capabilities Nodewise does not have).

Work criterion by criterion: score every use case on one criterion before moving to the next criterion. Write one line per score, in this order: all use cases on speed; all use cases on reuse; all use cases on pain; all use cases on moat; all use cases on fit.
